items: Clinical skills • Counselling station • Maternal and newborn care

blocks.text: You are the doctor on the postnatal ward. A woman who had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 24–48 hours ago is preparing to go home with her newborn.
Your task is to counsel her on:
Readiness for discharge.
Maternal recovery and personal hygiene.
Breastfeeding and newborn care.
Maternal and neonatal danger signs.
Immunisation and follow-up.
Postpartum contraception.
Emotional wellbeing and available support.

The examiner may also ask you to counsel a woman following caesarean section, instrumental delivery, postpartum haemorrhage, or a complicated pregnancy. In these situations, discharge depends on the woman's clinical condition and an individualised care plan.
Begin professionally and establish rapport.
Example opening:

“Good morning, Madam. My name is Dr ____. I understand that you and your baby may be preparing to go home today. I would like to discuss how you can look after yourself and your baby, the warning signs to watch for, and when to return to the hospital. Is that alright with you?”
Then:
Confirm the woman's identity and her baby's identity.
Ask how she is feeling physically and emotionally.
Ask whether she has any concerns about herself or the baby.
Assess her understanding of breastfeeding and newborn care.
Ask whether she has support at home and whether she can access a health facility if needed.
Use simple language and encourage questions.
Important: Do not assume that a woman is ready for discharge merely because a certain number of hours has elapsed since delivery.
Before discharge, confirm that the woman is clinically stable and that any complications have been appropriately managed.

rows: Stable temperature, pulse, respiratory rate and blood pressure
Lochia appropriate for the stage of recovery; no concerning heavy bleeding
Appropriate postpartum involution; no concerning uterine tenderness
Assess symptoms and needs, especially after surgery or severe perineal trauma
Controlled with an appropriate analgesic plan
No evidence of significant infection, wound breakdown or uncontrolled pain
Able to move safely, with appropriate support
Feeding plan established; breastfeeding support available if required
Emotional state assessed; urgent concerns addressed
Anaemia, hypertension, infection, haemorrhage or other conditions have an appropriate management and follow-up plan
Safe environment, access to help and a clear route back to care

blocks.text: A woman with persistent severe hypertension, fever, significant anaemia symptoms, uncontrolled pain, heavy bleeding or another unresolved complication may require further assessment or continued admission.
Confirm that the baby has been assessed and is suitable for discharge according to the facility's neonatal policy.
Breathing comfortably without significant respiratory distress.
Temperature stable.
Feeding effectively, with feeding difficulties assessed.
Passing urine and stool as appropriate for age.
No concerning jaundice or other signs of illness.
Weight and hydration assessed where indicated.
Newborn examination completed, with abnormalities addressed.
Required birth interventions, screening and immunisations reviewed according to local policy.
Parents can recognise danger signs and demonstrate essential newborn care.
Follow-up arrangements are clear.
Premature, low-birth-weight, jaundiced, unwell or otherwise high-risk babies may require additional monitoring or a specialised discharge plan.
Explain that vaginal bleeding after delivery is normal and usually gradually reduces and changes in colour over several weeks.
Initially, it is usually red.
It generally becomes pinkish or brownish.
Later, it may become pale or yellowish-white.
The pattern varies between women.
Advise her to seek urgent care if she experiences:
Sudden heavy bleeding or bleeding that rapidly soaks pads.
Large clots accompanied by heavy bleeding or feeling unwell.
Dizziness, fainting, marked weakness or palpitations.
Fever, worsening abdominal pain or foul-smelling discharge.
Do not reassure a woman with heavy bleeding simply because she is in the early postpartum period.
For a woman with an episiotomy or perineal tear:
Wash hands before and after toileting or wound care.
Clean the area gently with clean water.
Wipe from front to back.
Change sanitary pads regularly.
Avoid applying unprescribed creams, powders or antiseptics to the wound.
Take prescribed analgesics as directed.
Seek review for worsening pain, swelling, pus, wound separation or fever.
For a woman who underwent caesarean section:
Follow the wound-care instructions provided by the surgical team.
Keep the wound clean and follow advice on bathing and dressing changes.
Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity during recovery.
Mobilise regularly as advised to reduce complications associated with immobility.
Take prescribed medicines and attend the planned wound review.
Warning signs: Increasing wound redness, swelling, discharge, wound opening, fever, worsening abdominal pain or feeling systemically unwell.
Advise the woman to:
Drink fluids regularly unless medically restricted.
Eat a balanced diet containing fibre.
Mobilise as tolerated.
Avoid straining excessively during bowel movements.
Seek assessment for inability to pass urine, severe constipation, persistent vomiting or severe abdominal pain.
Resume activity gradually according to comfort and recovery.
Avoid prolonged immobility.
Accept practical help with cooking, cleaning and baby care.
Avoid driving until she can do so safely and comfortably, particularly after caesarean section or while taking sedating medication.
Resume sexual activity when physically and emotionally ready, bleeding and wounds have sufficiently settled, and any clinician-specific restrictions have been addressed.
There is no single mandatory date for resuming intercourse; comfort, healing, complications and personal preference matter.
Explain that exclusive breastfeeding is generally recommended for the first six months, followed by appropriate complementary feeding alongside continued breastfeeding.
Initiate breastfeeding early where possible and continue feeding responsively, whenever the baby shows hunger cues.
Look for early cues such as rooting, bringing hands to the mouth and increased alertness.
Ensure the baby's mouth takes in a good portion of the areola, not just the nipple.
Look for rhythmic sucking and swallowing.
Feed from one breast until the baby appears satisfied, then offer the other breast.
Avoid giving water or other feeds routinely to an exclusively breastfed newborn unless medically indicated.
Seek help for persistent nipple pain, poor latch, ineffective feeding or concerns about milk supply.
The baby attaches and sucks effectively.
Swallowing can be observed or heard.
The baby appears satisfied after many feeds.
Urine and stool output become appropriate for the baby's age.
Weight is monitored and progresses appropriately.
A newborn who is difficult to wake for feeds, repeatedly feeds ineffectively, has signs of dehydration or develops worsening jaundice needs prompt assessment.
Keep the umbilical stump clean and dry.
Fold the nappy below the stump.
Do not pull off the stump.
Do not apply ash, herbs, toothpaste, powders or other unprescribed substances.
Follow local guidance on chlorhexidine cord care where indicated.
Seek medical attention if there is spreading redness around the umbilicus, pus, a foul smell accompanied by inflammation, or the baby becomes unwell.
Keep the baby warm, especially in the first days of life.
Use skin-to-skin contact when appropriate and safe.
Dress the baby suitably for the environment without overheating.
Avoid placing the baby near open flames, hot objects or direct heat sources.
Counsel the parent to:
Place the baby on their back for every sleep.
Use a firm, flat sleep surface.
Keep pillows, loose blankets, toys and other soft objects out of the baby's sleep space.
Avoid overheating.
Keep the baby in the same room as the caregiver, ideally in a separate safe sleep space.
Avoid sleeping with the baby on a sofa or armchair.
Never shake a baby.
Delay the first bath until the baby is thermally stable; follow facility and national guidance.
Use warm water and keep the room comfortably warm.
Never leave the baby unattended in water, even briefly.
Clean the eyes and face gently.
Avoid inserting cotton buds or other objects into the ears or nose.
Explain that yellowing of the skin or eyes may occur in newborns, but it must not automatically be considered harmless.
Urgent assessment is required if:
Jaundice develops in the first 24 hours after birth.
Yellowing is increasing rapidly or becomes marked.
The baby is difficult to wake, feeds poorly or has an abnormal cry.
The palms or soles appear yellow.
There is fever, abnormal temperature, breathing difficulty or another sign of illness.
Jaundice assessment and bilirubin measurement should follow the baby's age in hours, gestational age and clinical risk factors.
Check the baby's immunisation record before discharge.
Explain vaccines already administered and those due next.
Give the caregiver the immunisation card and the next appointment date.
Follow the current Nigerian national immunisation schedule and local facility protocol.
Explain any planned newborn screening or preventive interventions.
Do not assume that every vaccine or screening test has been completed simply because the baby is being discharged.
This is a high-yield OSCE section. Explain when she must seek immediate medical attention.

rows: Heavy vaginal bleeding, fainting or collapse
Severe headache, blurred vision or seizures
Chest pain, sudden breathlessness or coughing blood
Pulmonary embolism or another cardiopulmonary emergency
Severe wound pain, redness or pus
Inability to pass urine or severe urinary symptoms
Severe confusion, hallucinations or thoughts of harming herself or the baby

blocks.text: Key counselling phrase:
“If you develop any of these symptoms, do not wait for your next appointment. Come to the hospital immediately or use the nearest emergency service.”
A postpartum woman can develop pre-eclampsia even if her blood pressure was normal during pregnancy.
Tell the mother to seek urgent medical attention if the baby:
Stops feeding or feeds markedly less than usual.
Is unusually sleepy, difficult to wake or floppy.
Has fast or difficult breathing, grunting or chest indrawing.
Has a fever or an abnormally low temperature.
Has convulsions or abnormal repetitive movements.
Develops jaundice within the first 24 hours or severe/progressive jaundice.
Vomits repeatedly, especially green vomit.
Has marked abdominal distension.
Has blue lips or tongue.
Has significantly reduced urine output or other signs of dehydration.
Develops redness spreading from the umbilicus or appears seriously unwell.
For a newborn, do not recommend waiting at home to see whether these signs resolve.
Explain that postnatal care is not limited to the discharge day.
The plan should include:
Maternal review of blood pressure, bleeding, pain, wound healing and any pregnancy-related complications.
Assessment of mood, sleep, coping and social support.
Breastfeeding assessment and support.
Newborn feeding, weight, hydration and jaundice assessment.
Review of immunisation and screening needs.
Contraception and future pregnancy planning.
A clear contact pathway if problems develop.

Arrange appointments according to national guidance, facility protocol and individual risk. Earlier review is needed for women with hypertension, diabetes, significant anaemia, infection, postpartum haemorrhage, caesarean complications or other concerns. Newborns discharged early or with feeding, weight or jaundice risks may need review within a short interval, sometimes within 24–48 hours.
Give the caregiver the actual appointment date, location and contact details rather than simply saying, “Come back later.”
Explain that pregnancy can occur before menstruation returns.
Discuss options according to the woman's preferences, medical eligibility, breastfeeding status and local availability. These may include:
Condoms.
Progestogen-only pills.
Implants.
Injectable contraception.
Intrauterine contraception, including appropriate postpartum timing.
Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM), if all criteria are met.
Other methods after assessing suitability and timing.
LAM is effective only when all three conditions are present:
The baby is younger than six months.
The mother has not resumed menstruation.
Breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive, frequent, including day and night.
If any condition no longer applies, she should use another contraceptive method if pregnancy is not desired.
Combined hormonal contraception may be unsuitable in the early postpartum period because of venous thromboembolism risk and requires assessment of breastfeeding and other risk factors.
Ask sensitively:

items: “How have you been feeling emotionally since delivery?”
“Do you have someone who can help you at home?”

blocks.text: “Have you been feeling persistently sad, hopeless or unable to cope?”

items: “Have you had any frightening thoughts or felt unsafe?”

blocks.text: Explain that emotional changes can occur after delivery, but persistent low mood, loss of interest, severe anxiety or difficulty functioning warrants assessment.

Urgent psychiatric assessment is required for hallucinations, delusions, severe confusion, mania, suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby. Do not leave a woman or baby at immediate risk without appropriate supervision and urgent help.
Encourage family members to support rest, nutrition, breastfeeding and attendance at follow-up appointments, while respecting the woman's autonomy and privacy.

subsections.subsection_title: Example of a complete OSCE counselling script

blocks.text: You may deliver the following summary at the end of the station:
“Madam, before you go home, we have checked that you and your baby are well enough for discharge and have discussed your care plan.

At home, eat a balanced diet, drink fluids regularly, rest when possible and gradually return to your normal activities. Your bleeding should generally reduce over time. Please seek urgent care if you develop heavy bleeding, fainting, severe headache, blurred vision, fever, worsening abdominal pain, chest pain or difficulty breathing.

Breastfeed your baby whenever the baby shows hunger cues and ask for help if feeding is painful or ineffective. Keep the cord clean and dry, keep your baby warm, and always place your baby on their back to sleep on a firm, flat surface.
If your baby develops difficulty breathing, fever or abnormally low temperature, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, convulsions or severe jaundice, bring the baby to the hospital urgently.

We will give you your follow-up appointments and immunisation information. We can also discuss contraception so that you can choose a method that suits you. Finally, please tell us if you feel persistently sad, overwhelmed or unsafe. You do not have to manage these difficulties alone.

items: What questions or concerns do you have before you leave?”

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What are the criteria for postnatal discharge?

Answer: Clinical stability of the mother, controlled pain, acceptable bleeding, no unresolved complication requiring admission, safe mobility and urination, an appropriate feeding plan, a newborn who is clinically suitable for discharge, caregiver education and documented follow-up.
Q2. Why must newborn follow-up be arranged after early discharge?
Answer: Newborns can develop feeding difficulties, dehydration, excessive weight loss, jaundice or infection after leaving the facility. Early review allows timely identification and intervention.
Q3. Can a woman develop pre-eclampsia after delivery?

Answer: Yes. Postpartum pre-eclampsia can occur after delivery, including in women who had no diagnosed hypertension during pregnancy. Severe headache, visual symptoms, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, breathlessness or seizures require urgent assessment.
Q4. What is the safest sleeping position for a newborn?
Answer: Supine — on the back — for every sleep, on a firm, flat sleep surface without loose bedding or soft objects.
Q5. What are the three criteria for LAM?
Answer: Infant younger than six months, maternal amenorrhoea and exclusive or nearly exclusive frequent breastfeeding.
Q6. What would prevent discharge of a newborn?

Answer: Any unresolved clinical instability, respiratory distress, temperature instability, suspected infection, ineffective feeding with concern about hydration, significant untreated jaundice, or another condition requiring continued observation or treatment.
Q7. What is the difference between routine follow-up and emergency review?

Answer: Routine follow-up monitors recovery, feeding, growth and preventive care. Emergency review is needed immediately for maternal or neonatal danger signs; the caregiver should not wait for a scheduled appointment.
Q8. What should you do if the mother says she cannot cope and has thoughts of harming herself?
Answer: Assess immediate risk, ensure she and the baby are safe, arrange urgent mental health assessment and appropriate supervision, and do not leave them alone if there is imminent danger.
Giving generic discharge advice without checking maternal and newborn readiness.
Forgetting postpartum hypertension and thromboembolism.
Failing to explain newborn danger signs.
Telling parents that jaundice is always normal.
Omitting safe sleep advice.
Forgetting immunisation documentation and follow-up dates.
Recommending LAM without checking all three criteria.
Ignoring maternal mood and family support.
Failing to explain where and how to seek urgent care.
Discharging a patient with unresolved complications without an appropriate plan.
Vitals, bleeding, pain, wounds and complications.
Breathing, temperature, feeding, jaundice and hydration.
Breastfeeding, nutrition, rest and hygiene.
Explain when and where to seek urgent care.
Cord care, warmth, hygiene and safe sleep.
Document dates, records and follow-up arrangements.
Contraception, emotional wellbeing and social support.
Invite questions and use teach-back to confirm comprehension.

Exam tip: Finish by asking the mother to explain in her own words which symptoms would make her return immediately. This demonstrates that you have checked her understanding rather than merely delivered information.
